title: Prediction and Quantification of Individual Athletic Performance of Runners
population: British runners from the thepowerof10 database: 164,746 individuals, 1,417,432 performances, 100 m to marathon
findings: Out-of-sample average prediction error of 3.6 min on elite marathon performances and 0.3 s on 100 m performances.
About 30% lower RMSE than the state of the art in performance prediction over a range of distances.
The model has three parameters per runner; the first component is a power law with a runner-dependent exponent that fits better than known power laws.

The authors argue Riegel's formula, Purdy points and the world-record power law can be explained within their findings, and that the per-runner parameters relate to training state, event specialisation and age.

Predictor trained on 164,746 individuals and 1,417,432 performances; out-of-sample average error e.g. 3.6 min on elite marathon performances and 0.3 s on 100 m, and a 30% RMSE improvement over the state of the art across distances.
The model has three parameters per runner and three shared components; the first component is a power law with a runner-dependent exponent that fits better than known power laws.

Documented phenomena (scoring tables, Riegel's formula, Purdy points, world-record power laws) may be explained on this basis; the authors present strong evidence that the three parameters relate to training state, event specialization and age, and state physiological hypotheses as conjecture.
limitations: Database of ranked UK (mostly club-level) runners, so skewed to competitive athletes; the quoted errors are for elite marathon performances and may not transfer to recreational or ultra runners; no environment or course adjustment; distances up to the marathon only.
implications: Replace a single fixed Riegel exponent with a runner-specific exponent estimated from that athlete's multi-distance results.
Use several race results rather than one anchor, and report prediction error in minutes per distance.
Do not quote the 3.6 min figure as expected accuracy for recreational runners.
Use a runner-specific exponent for cross-distance race projection instead of a fixed Riegel exponent, falling back to a default only when results exist at a single distance.
Treat predictions as goal ranges, widening uncertainty for distances far from recent races (e.g. ultras).
Age and event specialization should enter goal-time estimates as covariates.

verification.notes: Crossref (PLOS ONE, 2016-06-23, Blythe/Kiraly) and Europe PMC abstract re-fetched. Corrected the limitation text: the data is a public results database, not self-reported rankings.
